claims.text: The pinned Binance aggregate-trade response distinguishes q, quantity including all market trades, from nq, normal quantity excluding trades involving RPI orders. A SOL collector must preserve which quantity it uses; the fields do not describe the same flow population. (low confidence)

Bybit trade ingestion must not treat a repeated `seq` alone as a duplicate trade: the docs permit multiple messages for the same sequence and separately provide trade ID `i`. Preserve individual trade records and use the trade ID with instrument/venue context when designing deduplication. This is an implementation inference from the schema, not a documented SOL-specific data-loss incident. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Bybit book reconstruction replaces the local book when a new `snapshot` arrives and deletes a price level on zero size in a `delta`. Its documented service-restart update ID `u` equals 1 and requires overwriting the book. Treating every snapshot as new order inflow would contaminate a SOL book-flow feature; that contamination is an inference from the reset semantics. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

In the pinned Bybit documentation, ordinary orderbook messages exclude RPI orders, while the public trade schema has an RPI trade flag. Consequently, visible-book imbalance and executed flow have different coverage; their difference does not by itself identify a feed failure. (medium confidence)

Kim and Hansen explicitly state that their Binance aggregate-trade data lack matched contemporaneous quotes and use the latest transaction price as the opening reference. Their SOL-inclusive dataset therefore cannot alone establish a full-sample synchronized trade-and-book feature reconstruction. (low confidence)

For SOL perpetual flow pipelines that use these venue schemas, normalize aggressor direction from the venue fields rather than price changes: Binance defines `m` as whether the buyer is the market maker, whereas Bybit defines `S` as the taker side. Thus buyer-maker true denotes sell aggression on Binance; Bybit Buy denotes buy aggression. This is a schema-based mapping, not an empirically established SOL trading edge. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

A message count is not a comparable trade-count feature across these feeds: Binance aggregates same-price, same-taking-side fills every 100 milliseconds; Bybit says a futures/spot message may contain up to 1024 trades and multiple messages may share the same sequence. For SOL measurements, aggregate signed trade size over explicitly matched windows instead of counting WebSocket messages; this last step is a methodological recommendation. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Bybit instructs consumers to replace the local book on each new snapshot. Delta quantities equal to 0 delete a level, absent levels are inserted, and existing levels are updated. This is an implementation requirement for reconstructing SOL book features, rather than evidence that a particular SOL collector follows it. (low confidence)

Bybit distinguishes system-generation time `ts` from matching-engine book time `cts`; it explicitly permits correlating `cts` with public-trade `T`, the fill timestamp. A SOL trade/book join should therefore preserve these separate clocks rather than silently treating message-generation and matching times as interchangeable; that join rule is a methodological inference. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

Bookmap argues that grouping small trades can make activity appear as one large aggressive trade. Treat this as an attributed vendor caution about trade-size features; the article provides an illustrative mechanism rather than an estimated SOL aggregation error. (low confidence)

Displayed-book and executed-trade universes require explicit alignment: Bybit excludes RPI orders from its public book but flags RPI trades in the trade stream; Binance distinguishes all-market quantity `q` from normal quantity `nq` excluding trades involving RPI orders. Consequently, a SOL trade-versus-displayed-depth feature needs a stated RPI inclusion policy; the policy requirement is an inference, not proof that a particular SOL sample contains RPI activity. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

The cited Tardis documentation snapshot describes REST-generated initial Binance futures book snapshots, continuity checks using `pu` and `u`, and reconnection after a missed message. The cited Bybit documentation snapshot instructs consumers to reset the book after new snapshots. For SOL replay based on these documented conventions, label invalid or rebuilding intervals separately from zero flow and preserve snapshot provenance. This is a recommended control rather than a measured SOL outage rate. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-09)

HFT Architecture reports a SOL-perpetual measurement sensitivity in its July 2026 sample: with Binance represented by trades rather than its book, explained Bybit variation falls from 13.1% to 2.3%; the authors attribute this to bid/ask bounce and multi-level executions. This is the authors' bounded observational result, not an independently replicated estimate, a current venue ranking, or evidence of profitable CVD/OFI prediction. (low confidence)

Bybit documents seq as a way to compare orderbook levels, with smaller seq meaning earlier generation. It also documents repeated level-one snapshots with the same u after 3 seconds without changes. These semantics scope gap detectors: a repeated u does not necessarily mean dropped SOL updates. (low confidence)

The pinned NautilusTrader Binance adapter documentation checks Futures continuation using pu == previous u. On a sequence gap it stops book output, buffers diffs, and requests a fresh snapshot. This is a concrete implementation pattern for withholding reconstructed features during a gap, not a measured SOL outage rate. (low confidence)

The pinned NautilusTrader adapter documentation says QuoteTick ts_event differs by transport: Spot SBE uses an event timestamp, Spot JSON bookTicker can fall back to ts_init, and Futures uses transaction time. A unified field name therefore does not guarantee identical timestamp provenance across the inputs to a SOL comparison. (low confidence)

CCXT explains that contract counts multiplied by contractSize give base quantity. This is a normalization check for contract-denominated SOL inputs, not proof that every venue native trade-size field is a contract count. (low confidence)

Kim and Hansen report using Binance perpetual aggregate trades including Solana (SOL), covering January 1, 2021 through October 31, 2024. They report rare missing-data episodes in the official files, corrected by March 16, 2026, and describe them as negligible for their own analysis. This supports tracking historical-file revisions; it does not quantify present SOL stream loss. (low confidence)

Kim and Hansen describe the Bybit replication in their additional robustness checks as BTC and ETH maps. That particular replication is not a SOL cross-venue validation, even though the Binance sample includes SOL. (low confidence)

In the historical Tardis discussion, a commenter warns that a VM timestamp can have jitter far above its stated precision and cautions against treating the added timestamp as authoritative. This is an attributed implementation concern, not a measured SOL latency estimate. (low confidence)

Sensitivity to collection clock and feed representation belongs in SOL validation: the SOL-containing HFT Architecture study distinguishes Tokyo receipt time from exchange timestamps and warns that exchange clocks are not synchronized; Tardis records local timestamps alongside raw exchange messages. Recommended tests retain both timestamps and compare book-based and trade-based results before asserting a cross-venue lead; neither source establishes a universal SOL clock-correction constant. (medium confidence)
